old:
Economics applies the scientific method — observation, hypothesis formation, testing, refinement — to human behaviour and societies.

Unlike the natural sciences it cannot run controlled laboratory experiments, so economists build models resting on simplifying assumptions and test them against real-world data. Different assumptions can lead economists to different conclusions from the same data.
new:

Unlike the natural sciences it cannot run controlled laboratory experiments, so economists build models resting on simplifying assumptions and test them against real-world data.

old:
The central purpose of economic activity is the production of goods and services to satisfy needs and wants.

Needs — basic requirements for human survival, such as food, water and shelter. Wants — desires for goods and services that improve quality of life, such as entertainment and travel.
new:
The central purpose of economic activity is the production of goods and services to satisfy needs and wants.

  • Needs — basic requirements for human survival, such as food, water and shelter.
  • Wants — desires for goods and services that improve quality of life, such as entertainment and travel.

old:
The environment provides essential goods and services — clean air, water, fertile land — and overconsumption can leave it degraded, harming future economic activity, so it must be managed sustainably.

Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced once used (fossil fuels, minerals). Renewable resources replenish naturally (forests, fish stocks) but can still become scarce if overused or mismanaged.
new:
The environment provides essential goods and services — clean air, water, fertile land — and overconsumption can leave it degraded, harming future economic activity, so it must be managed sustainably.

  • Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced once used (fossil fuels, minerals).
  • Renewable resources replenish naturally (forests, fish stocks) but can still become scarce if overused or mismanaged.

old: Points on the frontier (A, C, D, B) are productively efficient — all resources fully and efficiently used. Point E inside the frontier means unemployed or inefficiently used resources: more of both goods is possible at zero opportunity cost. Point F outside is currently unattainable with existing resources and technology. A movement along the frontier, such as C to D, shows the opportunity cost of producing more consumer goods.
new:
• Points on the frontier (A, C, D, B) are productively efficient — all resources fully and efficiently used.
  • Point E inside the frontier means unemployed or inefficiently used resources: more of both goods is possible at zero opportunity cost.
  • Point F outside is currently unattainable with existing resources and technology.

A movement along the frontier, such as C to D, shows the opportunity cost of producing more consumer goods.

old:
Utility — the satisfaction or happiness a consumer derives from consuming goods and services.

Total utility — the total satisfaction from consuming a given quantity. Marginal utility — the additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit.
new:
Utility — the satisfaction or happiness a consumer derives from consuming goods and services.

  • Total utility — the total satisfaction from consuming a given quantity.
  • Marginal utility — the additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit.

old: A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price — an extension when price falls, a contraction when it rises. A shift (D1 to D2) is caused by a non-price factor: real incomes (normal vs inferior goods), tastes and advertising, the price of substitutes or complements, or population changes.
new:
A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price — an extension when price falls, a contraction when it rises.

A shift (D1 to D2) is caused by a non-price factor:

  • Real incomes (normal vs inferior goods).
  • Tastes and advertising.
  • The price of substitutes or complements.
  • Population changes.

old: PED is negative for a normal demand curve — classify on the magnitude: 0 = perfectly inelastic; between 0 and 1 = relatively inelastic; 1 = unitary; above 1 = relatively elastic; infinity = perfectly elastic.
new:
PED is negative for a normal demand curve — classify on the magnitude:

  • 0 = perfectly inelastic.
  • Between 0 and 1 = relatively inelastic.
  • 1 = unitary.
  • Above 1 = relatively elastic.
  • Infinity = perfectly elastic.

old: A movement along the curve comes only from a change in the good's own price — an extension when price rises, a contraction when it falls. A shift (S1 to S2) comes from a non-price factor changing costs or capacity: production costs, indirect taxes, subsidies, technology, the number of firms in the market, or external shocks.
new:
A movement along the curve comes only from a change in the good's own price — an extension when price rises, a contraction when it falls.

A shift (S1 to S2) comes from a non-price factor changing costs or capacity:

  • Production costs.
  • Indirect taxes.
  • Subsidies.
  • Technology.
  • The number of firms in the market.
  • External shocks.

old:
PES — measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's own price: how easily, quickly or cheaply producers can increase output when the price rises.

0 = perfectly inelastic (vertical supply curve); between 0 and 1 = relatively inelastic; above 1 = relatively elastic; infinity = perfectly elastic (horizontal).
new:
PES — measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's own price: how easily, quickly or cheaply producers can increase output when the price rises.

  • 0 = perfectly inelastic (vertical supply curve).
  • Between 0 and 1 = relatively inelastic.
  • Above 1 = relatively elastic.
  • Infinity = perfectly elastic (horizontal).

old:
Time is the main determinant. Others: spare production capacity, ease of storing stocks, mobility of factors of production, complexity of production, the marginal cost of extra units, and the availability of raw materials.

Short run — at least one factor of production is fixed, so supply is more price inelastic. Long run — all factors are variable, so supply is more price elastic.
new:
Time is the main determinant. Others:

  • Spare production capacity.
  • Ease of storing stocks.
  • Mobility of factors of production.
  • Complexity of production.
  • The marginal cost of extra units.
  • The availability of raw materials.

Short run — at least one factor of production is fixed, so supply is more price inelastic.

Long run — all factors are variable, so supply is more price elastic.

old:
Productivity measures the efficiency of production: output per unit of input. Labour productivity is output per worker (or per worker per hour).

Higher productivity means lower costs per unit, higher profits and a competitive edge — which is why it recurs across the whole specification.
new:
Productivity measures the efficiency of production: output per unit of input.

Labour productivity is output per worker (or per worker per hour).

Higher productivity means lower costs per unit, higher profits and a competitive edge — which is why it recurs throughout the course.

old:
Marginal returns: the extra output from one more unit of a variable factor (ΔTotal output ÷ ΔInputs). Average returns: output per unit of the variable factor. Total returns: total output.

In the short run, adding a variable factor to a fixed one eventually yields smaller and smaller additions to output — more bartenders behind a fixed bar get in each other's way. This is what makes the MC curve fall and then rise.
new:
• Marginal returns: the extra output from one more unit of a variable factor (ΔTotal output ÷ ΔInputs).
  • Average returns: output per unit of the variable factor.
  • Total returns: total output.

In the short run, adding a variable factor to a fixed one eventually yields smaller and smaller additions to output — more bartenders behind a fixed bar get in each other's way.

This is what makes the MC curve fall and then rise.

old:
In the long run all factors are variable, so the firm can change its whole scale. Increasing returns to scale: output rises more than proportionately to inputs. Constant: proportionately. Decreasing: less than proportionately.

Returns to scale underpin economies and diseconomies of scale — the long-run counterpart to the short run's diminishing returns.
new:
In the long run all factors are variable, so the firm can change its whole scale.

  • Increasing returns to scale: output rises more than proportionately to inputs.
  • Constant: proportionately.
  • Decreasing: less than proportionately.

Returns to scale underpin economies and diseconomies of scale — the long-run counterpart to the short run's diminishing returns.

old:
Fixed costs do not vary with output (rent, salaries); variable costs do (materials, hourly wages). TC = TFC + TVC.

The averages divide by output: AC = TC ÷ Q, AFC = TFC ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q. MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the cost of one more unit, and the curve that drives all the others.
new:
• Fixed costs do not vary with output (rent, salaries).
  • Variable costs do (materials, hourly wages).
  • TC = TFC + TVC.

The averages divide by output:

  • AC = TC ÷ Q.
  • AFC = TFC ÷ Q.
  • AVC = TVC ÷ Q.

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the cost of one more unit, and the curve that drives all the others.

old:
TC = 150 + TVC: 240, 300, 390, 540

AC = TC ÷ Q: 240 ÷ 10 = £24; 300 ÷ 20 = £15; 390 ÷ 30 = £13; 540 ÷ 40 = £13.50

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ: (300 − 240) ÷ 10 = £6; then £9; then £15

AC bottoms at £13 and turns upward between 30 and 40 units — exactly where MC (£15) rises above it.
new:
TC = 150 + TVC: 240, 300, 390, 540

AC = TC ÷ Q:

  • 240 ÷ 10 = £24
  • 300 ÷ 20 = £15
  • 390 ÷ 30 = £13
  • 540 ÷ 40 = £13.50

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ:

  • (300 − 240) ÷ 10 = £6
  • then £9
  • then £15

AC bottoms at £13 and turns upward between 30 and 40 units — exactly where MC (£15) rises above it.

old:
Size itself raises average costs: communication and managerial strain (messages distorted across layers), motivational problems (workers feel unnoticed — the principal-agent link) and geographical coordination across distant sites.

They are not diminishing returns: diseconomies are a long-run phenomenon of scale with all factors variable, while diminishing returns is a short-run law that needs a fixed factor.
new:
Size itself raises average costs:

  • Communication and managerial strain (messages distorted across layers).
  • Motivational problems (workers feel unnoticed — the principal-agent link).
  • Geographical coordination across distant sites.

They are not diminishing returns: diseconomies are a long-run phenomenon of scale with all factors variable, while diminishing returns is a short-run law that needs a fixed factor.

old: TR = P × Q, the firm's total earnings. AR = TR ÷ Q — the price per unit, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve. MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, the extra revenue from one more unit.
new:
• TR = P × Q, the firm's total earnings.
  • AR = TR ÷ Q — the price per unit, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve.
  • MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, the extra revenue from one more unit.

old:
Normal profit is the minimum profit required to keep a firm in the industry: TR = TC, the break-even point — counted as a cost, because it is the entrepreneur's opportunity cost of staying. Abnormal (supernormal) profit is anything above that (TR > TC); a loss is TR < TC.

Profit is maximised at the output where MC = MR.
new:
Normal profit is the minimum profit required to keep a firm in the industry: TR = TC, the break-even point — counted as a cost, because it is the entrepreneur's opportunity cost of staying.

Abnormal (supernormal) profit is anything above that (TR > TC); a loss is TR < TC.

Profit is maximised at the output where MC = MR.

old: Profit is the market's engine: an incentive for entrepreneurs to take risks, a signal drawing resources to where they are most valued, a source of reinvestment that funds growth and innovation, a driver of competition pushing prices down and quality up, and the reward to investors for the capital they risk.
new:
Profit is the market's engine:

  • An incentive for entrepreneurs to take risks.
  • A signal drawing resources to where they are most valued.
  • A source of reinvestment that funds growth and innovation.
  • A driver of competition pushing prices down and quality up.
  • The reward to investors for the capital they risk.

old:
Collusion is firms agreeing — formally or informally — to restrict supply and raise price, acting like a monopoly to earn supernormal profit. Overt collusion is a formal agreement (a cartel): illegal and provable in court, as when British Airways and Virgin Atlantic fixed fuel surcharges in 2007.

Tacit collusion is an informal understanding, often via price leadership — the market leader sets a price and rivals follow. Same outcome, far harder to prove.
